title: Continuity of a Function (Intuitive Definition)
notes: **Intuitive definition:** A function f is continuous on an interval [a,b] if its graph is a smooth curve without any breaks in that interval.
**Visual interpretation:** The curve can be drawn by continuous motion of a pencil without lifting it from the paper.
**Contrast with discontinuity:** A discontinuous function has breaks, jumps, or holes in its graph.
**Key requirement:** There are no abrupt changes, gaps, or undefined points in the interval.
**Examples of continuous functions:** Polynomials, sine, cosine, exponential functions are continuous everywhere.
**Examples of discontinuous functions:** Functions with vertical asymptotes or jump discontinuities.
**Physical analogy:** Continuous motion vs. teleportation — continuous functions have no 'jumps' in value.
**Mathematical basis:** Intuitive continuity leads to the formal definition involving limits.
confusion: Intuitive continuity is not the same as formal continuity — the intuitive version lacks precision.
A function can look continuous but have a removable discontinuity (hole) that's hard to see.
Don't confuse continuity with differentiability — continuous functions may not be smooth (e.g., |x| at 0).
Intervals matter — a function can be continuous on [a,b] but discontinuous outside that interval.
Visual inspection can be misleading; formal limit conditions are needed for rigorous analysis.

universalFacts: Continuity is one of the most fundamental concepts in calculus and analysis.
Continuous functions have important properties: they achieve maximum and minimum values on closed intervals.
The intermediate value theorem applies to continuous functions on closed intervals.
Most physical quantities (temperature, position, velocity) vary continuously in nature.
Computer graphics use continuous functions to create smooth curves and surfaces.
